In the career cell's waiting room, Farida had filled in the consulting firm's form in neat capitals. The package would clear her father's loan in three years.
"You hate spreadsheets," Aditi said, reading over her shoulder.
"Abbu took that loan for my fees. Ammi sold her bangles. I owe them everything."
"You do owe them something," Aditi said. "But is it this exact job, or is it you being okay?"
Farida pressed her pen until it clicked. "If I take the public-health fellowship, the money's half. I'd feel like I'm throwing away what they did."
"Or you'd be the daughter who does work she believes in and still sends money home. Different, not ungrateful."
When the counsellor called her in, Farida laid both forms on the desk. "Can we look at how I could do the fellowship and still help with the loan? Maybe tutoring on weekends?" The counsellor pulled out a notepad. Farida's shoulders came down an inch.

qa.a: In three years.

qa.q: What does Farida pressing her pen until it clicked suggest?
qa.a: She felt tense and guilty, torn between repaying her parents and the fellowship she actually wanted.

qa.q: What did Farida do instead of choosing only out of guilt?
qa.a: She took both forms to the counsellor and asked how to manage the fellowship while still helping with the loan, for example by tutoring on weekends.

qa.a: As real but not tied to one job; Aditi thinks Farida can repay in a different form without being ungrateful.

grounding: Shows feeling you owe your parents your life, and seeing that gratitude and repayment can take other forms than the path they hoped for.

Dear Mummy,
I'm writing because on the phone I only ever say "all good".
You worked double shifts at the hospital for eleven years so I could study in Delhi. Papa sold his scooter. I think about that every day, and for three years it's been the reason I kept going with CA, even though I've failed the intermediate twice and dread every page.
I've told myself that if I quit, your sacrifice would be wasted. But I think I've been disappearing into what I thought you wanted, just so I wouldn't feel guilty.
The thing I'm good at, the thing I lose track of time doing, is cooking. I've been working weekends in a café kitchen, and the head chef, Gurleen, says I should apply for the hotel management course.
I'm not asking you to be happy about it yet. I'm asking you to let me show you. I'll still send money when I can. I'll still be your son who owes you everything, just not in the shape you imagined.
Sachin

qa.a: For eleven years.

qa.a: Guilt: he felt that quitting would waste his parents' sacrifice, even though he dreads every page.

Every family function, Mehr, it's the same line: "Samir got 94 per cent, Samir's at IIT, Samir's getting a big package." And then my mother looks at me like I'm a purchase she regrets.
For two years I hated Samir. I mean it. I'd leave the room when he came in. Poor guy, he never did anything except exist.
Then at Diwali, after the fourth comparison in one evening, I went into the kitchen and said to Mummy, quietly, "When you compare me to Samir, it hurts. I'm working hard. I just don't do it his way." She got defensive, then went quiet, then said, "I just get scared you'll be left behind. Everyone asks me."
That's when it clicked. It wasn't really about my marks. It was about her fear.
She still slips. But now I say, "Mummy, Samir again?" and she laughs. And I actually talked to Samir at the last wedding. He's nice. He hates the comparisons too.
I'm Rekha, by the way, the cousin who isn't at IIT.

qa.a: At IIT.

qa.a: Resentful, even hating him and leaving the room whenever he came in.

qa.a: Told Mummy quietly in the kitchen that the comparison hurts, which brought out Mummy's real fear.

The offer from the Bengaluru firm had to be accepted by 6 p.m., and it was already 4:30 when Madhuri finally got her mother on a crackling line from Nani's village.
"Beta, stay in Nagpur. Your father's cousin can get you into the bank here."
Madhuri's first instinct was to say, "You don't understand my field," and hang up. Her sister Simran, beside her, raised an eyebrow.
"Mummy, can I ask why you want me here? Really why."
The line crackled. "When I was twenty-two I went to Pune alone and was so lonely I cried every night. I don't want that for you."
Madhuri swallowed. "Thank you for telling me. I didn't know that. I still think Bengaluru is right for me. I'll find a PG with girls from my team, call you every night, and if I'm miserable after six months, I'll tell you honestly."
Silence, then: "You're an adult. Just call."
At 5:48 she clicked accept, Simran cheering beside her.

Every time Layla's father transferred her rent to her Lyon account, he added a message: "Remember who is paying." Every time, she swallowed what she wanted to say about her history degree, her friends, anything at all.

Last month I asked your roommate to tell me when you came back each night, and I checked your location every hour. When your mid-term marks came, I posted them in the family group and wrote, "See what happens in hostel." You haven't really talked to me since.

First salary day!
27,000 in my account. I stared at the number on the office bus like it might disappear.
By 8 p.m. Mummy had called twice, once to say how proud she is, once to mention the electricity bill and Darshan's coaching fees. Darshan texted, "Didi, new phone? 😄"
The old me would have sent almost everything home by midnight, just so nobody could think I'd changed, and then borrowed from my roommate by the 20th. Or I'd have said nothing and quietly kept it all.
Instead I sat down with a notebook and made columns: rent, food, travel, a small line for emergencies, and a share for home. Then I called Mummy and told her what I could send every month, and why I was keeping some for rent and emergencies. She was quiet, then said, "That's fair. You're living alone."
Darshan is not getting a new phone. He got a chocolate cake.
— Bhavna
